# Oblio Data Model: *objectStruct*, *recordStruct*, and *fieldStruct* Reference

**Introduction:** The Oblio project’s data model combines *intensional* schema design with an Entity–Attribute–Value (EAV) framework, while preserving Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) principles. In this model, **objectStruct**, **fieldStruct**, and **recordStruct** are core concepts that capture the schema (metadata) and instance data of an open-ended database. This reference manual provides a formal, comprehensive description of these terms and their relationships. The goal is to enable an AI agent or reasoning engine to fully grasp the data model – including its abstract roles, constraints, and semantics – for tasks like logical reasoning, schema evolution, or generative code design.

**Overview of Components:** At a high level, the model resembles a classic EAV schema[\[1\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=)[\[2\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=Stores%20the%20possible%20attributes%20that,an%20entity%20can%20have). An *objectStruct* represents an entity *type* or class (the intensional schema component), a *fieldStruct* represents an *attribute definition* (a property that instances of an objectStruct can have), and a *recordStruct* represents an *entity instance* or record (the extensional data, grouping specific values of fields for one object). The relationships are roughly: an **objectStruct** *defines* a set of **fieldStructs** (attributes) and can have many **recordStructs** (instances), while each **recordStruct** is an instance *of* one objectStruct and contains values for the relevant fieldStructs. This separation of schema and data allows new object types or fields to be introduced at runtime without altering the underlying table structure[\[3\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=Stores%20the%20possible%20attributes%20that,an%20entity%20can%20have), achieving a highly flexible, “open” schema design[\[4\]](https://www.dremio.com/wiki/entity-attribute-value-model/#:~:text=In%20the%20EAV%20model%2C%20data,in%20storing%20and%20retrieving%20data).

![][image1]  
*Figure 1: Illustration of an Entity–Attribute–Value style schema (from a content management example) mapped to Oblio’s terms. Here* ContentType *(analogous to* *objectStruct) defines a category of content and its fields;* Attribute *(analogous to* *fieldStruct) defines a property name and type for a ContentType;* Content *(analogous to* *recordStruct) is an instance of a ContentType; and* ContentAttributeValue *stores each (Content, Attribute, Value) triple. This flexible structure allows dynamic addition of new fields and object types without schema changes[\[1\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=)[\[2\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=Stores%20the%20possible%20attributes%20that,an%20entity%20can%20have).*

## **objectStruct** (Object Type Definition)

**Role & Definition:** An **objectStruct** represents an abstract *entity type* or *object class* in the Oblio data model. It defines a *schema blueprint* for a category of objects – much like a class in OOP or an entity in a traditional ER model – but is stored and manipulated as data (intensional schema). In other words, an objectStruct encapsulates the intentional schema information: it names the entity type and enumerates which fields (attributes) that type can have[\[1\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=)[\[2\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=Stores%20the%20possible%20attributes%20that,an%20entity%20can%20have). Conceptually, one can think of each objectStruct as defining a custom “table” structure or object definition at runtime. Every **recordStruct** (instance) will explicitly reference an objectStruct to indicate its type, meaning the objectStruct acts as the *type tag* or class identifier for records.

**Structural Constraints:** Each objectStruct typically has a unique identifier (such as a type ID or name) that distinguishes it from other types. The structure of an objectStruct includes: (a) a **Name** or label (unique across all objectStructs) identifying the entity type (e.g. “Person”, “Product”, “Event”), and (b) a **Field List** – the set of fieldStructs that belong to this objectStruct. The objectStruct is thus essentially a container for a collection of field definitions. There may also be optional metadata like a description or version, but at minimum it defines a set of allowed fields. By design, an objectStruct can own *zero or more* fieldStructs (though in practice usually at least one field is defined). No two fieldStructs within the same objectStruct share the same name (field names are unique per object type), ensuring a well-defined schema for that type. Each objectStruct may impose additional structural constraints on its fields (for example, designating some fields as a primary key or required fields – more on these invariants below).

**Relationships and Composition:** The relationship between objectStructs and the other components is hierarchical and referential:

* **Composition with fieldStruct:** An objectStruct *composes* multiple fieldStructs. Formally, there is a one-to-many relationship: each objectStruct O has a set of fieldStructs {f1, f2, ... fn} that are defined for O. Every fieldStruct is owned by exactly one objectStruct (its defining entity type). This means if fieldStruct F is associated with objectStruct O, F cannot exist independently or belong to a different objectStruct – it is a property specific to O. For example, if objectStruct \= Person, it might have fieldStructs like Name, BirthDate, etc., and those fields inherently apply to Person records only.

* **Association with recordStruct:** An objectStruct is also associated with the set of recordStructs that are instances of that type. There is a one-to-many relationship here as well: each objectStruct O can have many recordStruct instances (0, 1, or many) that claim O as their type, whereas each recordStruct points to exactly one objectStruct as its type. In other words, objectStructs classify recordStructs. For example, the Person objectStruct may have numerous recordStruct instances representing individual persons in the data. This association is typically implemented by storing a type reference (foreign key to objectStruct) in each recordStruct.

* **Referencing between objectStructs:** The model can potentially support relationships between different objectStructs (akin to foreign key relations in a relational model or object references in ORM). However, such relationships would be realized through special fieldStructs whose value type is another objectStruct (see **fieldStruct** below for details on reference types). For instance, if Company and Person are objectStructs, one might define a fieldStruct in Person like employer that references a Company recordStruct. This creates an inter-objectStruct reference (one-to-many or many-to-many via a linking structure) but does not break the rule that each fieldStruct belongs to a single objectStruct (in this case, the field employer belongs to Person type and holds an identifier of a Company instance). ObjectStructs themselves do not contain other objectStructs hierarchically (unless a subclassing or inheritance mechanism is introduced), but conceptually one could model inheritance by having an objectStruct with a special field that references another objectStruct’s key, or by the agent treating certain sets of fields as shared patterns.

**Invariants and Schema Constraints:** Several important invariants govern objectStructs to maintain a normalized, consistent schema:

* **Field Ownership:** *All fieldStructs referenced by an objectStruct must list that objectStruct as their owner.* Equivalently, an objectStruct’s field list can only include fields that are defined for that objectStruct. If by some error a record references a field outside its objectStruct, that would violate the schema (this situation should be prevented by design – see **recordStruct** invariants).

* **Unique Type Names/IDs:** Every objectStruct should have a unique identity (like a unique name or ID). No two objectStructs share the same identifier or name. This ensures clarity when referencing types and prevents ambiguity in queries or code generation.

* **Unique Field Names per Type:** Within a given objectStruct, each fieldStruct must have a unique name (or key). This is analogous to column names being unique within a database table. It prevents collision and allows referring to a field by name within the context of its object type. (Different objectStructs can reuse field names coincidentally, but those would be distinct fieldStruct entries – e.g., two object types might both have a field named “Title”, but internally these are separate fieldStructs tied to different objectStructs.)

* **Optional vs Required Fields:** The schema can mark certain fieldStructs as *required* for that object type. A required field means every recordStruct of this type **must** have a value for that field (the absence of a value would violate a constraint). Conversely, fields not marked required are optional – a record may omit them (treated as missing/unknown if not present). This constraint is intensional (part of objectStruct definition) but has implications in the extensional data (recordStructs must comply – see recordStruct invariants).

* **Key or Identity Fields:** ObjectStructs may designate one or more fieldStructs as forming a primary key or unique identifier for instances (aside from the implicit record ID). For example, an objectStruct “Person” might use a combination of “FirstName+LastName+BirthDate” or a national ID number field as a unique key. If such key fields are defined, the model must enforce uniqueness across all recordStructs of that type. (Uniqueness is usually an invariant on fieldStruct definitions – see **fieldStruct invariants** – but since it constrains records of that object type, it’s also part of the objectStruct’s overall schema rules).

* **Type Hierarchy (if any):** By default, objectStructs in this model are peers without inheritance, but if the design were extended to allow subtyping (an objectStruct inheriting fields from another), certain invariants would apply (like a subtype’s fields \= parent’s fields ∪ additional fields, etc.). However, unless explicitly supported, we assume no inheritance among objectStructs in Oblio (each objectStruct is a standalone definition). Instead, relationships between types are handled via reference fields or composition rather than subclassing.

* **Normalization & Minimal Redundancy:** The separation of objectStructs and fieldStructs is a meta-model normalization. Each objectStruct defines its fields in one place (in the fieldStruct list). Field definitions are not duplicated for each record – instead, recordStructs simply reference these definitions when storing values. This design mirrors the EAV approach: *the attribute metadata is stored once*, and *each attribute-value pair is stored as a separate fact linked to that metadata*, rather than as separate columns[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=Data%20is%20recorded%20as%20three,columns)[\[6\]](https://dzone.com/articles/custom-attributes-in-relational-databases#:~:text=Concept). This avoids schema duplication and allows easy evolution (adding/dropping fields by updating objectStruct and fieldStruct tables). It implicitly ensures that *all instances of a given objectStruct share the same field definitions*, keeping the schema consistent across records of the same type.

**Behavior and Query Semantics:** An objectStruct, being schema information, is primarily interacted with when *defining or modifying* the schema and when *interpreting queries* about records:

* **Defining New Types:** Creating a new objectStruct at runtime (intensional addition) is the mechanism for introducing a new category of entity. An AI agent can generate a new objectStruct with a set of fieldStructs to adapt the schema for new data requirements without a migration. The system must ensure any new objectStruct receives a unique identifier and that any new fieldStructs under it don’t clash with existing field names in that type.

* **Schema Introspection:** Agents or queries can ask “what fields does objectStruct X have?” or “what is the data type of field Y in type X?”. Because schema is data, such queries are answered by looking up fieldStruct entries associated with the objectStruct. This is akin to introspecting an ORM class definition or a database information schema at runtime. For instance, a reasoning engine might use this to dynamically decide how to handle a record of an unknown type by inspecting its objectStruct definition (e.g., to generate UI forms or to validate input fields).

* **Querying Instances by Type:** When retrieving or filtering data, objectStruct acts like a type filter. A query like “find all records of type *Person* where Age \> 30” first identifies the objectStruct for “Person”, then finds all recordStructs of that type with an associated Age field value \> 30\. In SQL/EAV terms, one would join the record table with the values table and the field meta table, etc., or in logic terms, constrain the Type(record) \= PersonType. Because the object type is explicitly stored per record, queries can efficiently select by type. Moreover, the agent can reason that certain fields only exist for certain types (e.g., it would not look for a “Salary” field on a record of type “Event” if Salary is defined only for type “Job”).

* **Continuous/Incremental Schema Updates:** Under a *continuous truth* model, the set of objectStructs and fieldStructs can evolve over time, and an AI agent may receive updates about new or modified types. The agent should treat the definitions in objectStruct as facts that can change (especially in a development or generative design setting). For example, if a new field is added to objectStruct *Product*, any subsequent reasoning about Product records should include that field (even if older records lack it). This requires the agent to handle **partial knowledge** gracefully: at time T1, the agent might not know about a field (truth about its existence was unknown); at time T2, a fieldStruct is added (making that schema element true/available going forward). The agent should incorporate this new schema element into its model of the world without inconsistency. Similarly, if an objectStruct is deprecated or fields removed, the agent must update its knowledge base and possibly interpret past records accordingly (e.g., treat removed fields as no longer applicable to new records, but historical data might still have those values).

* **Open World vs. Closed World Assumption:** Because objectStruct defines what *could* be true for records (i.e., what fields *could* exist), there is an interesting semantic nuance: In a **closed-world** scenario typical of relational databases, if a field is not present for a record, one might assume a default or “no value” as definitive. However, if we adopt an **open-world assumption** (as many AI reasoning systems do[\[7\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/open-world-assumption#:~:text=Open%20World%20Assumption%20in%20computer,model%20elements%20is%20not%20guaranteed)), the absence of a field value is treated as *unknown* rather than *false*. The objectStruct doesn’t necessarily assert that every field must have a value (unless marked required); it only enumerates the potential properties. Thus, an agent might reason: “Given objectStruct Person with field MiddleName, a particular Person record without a MiddleName value isn’t proof that the person has no middle name – it might simply be unknown or not provided.” Under open-world semantics, knowledge about that field for the record is incomplete. In contrast, under closed-world (or if the field were explicitly set to null/none meaning “no value”), one could infer the person truly has no middle name. The design of Oblio leans toward *partial knowledge management*: it’s designed to allow storing what is known and leaving other fields unspecified. The reasoning agent must be careful to distinguish *“missing because false/none”* vs *“missing because unknown”*. By default, missing field values in an EAV model mean *“not recorded (yet)”*, aligning with an open-world approach where facts not in the database are not automatically false[\[8\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/computer-science/open-world-assumption#:~:text=In%20contrast%2C%20ontologies%20are%20based,measured%20for%20the%20segment%20of). This suits AI scenarios where knowledge is accumulated continuously.

* **Schema Versioning and Truth Maintenance:** If schema can change over time (e.g., a field is added or its constraints change), the truth of statements involving that schema may also change. For example, a rule like “all records of type T have at most 5 fields” could become false if a sixth fieldStruct is added to T. An AI agent using a truth-maintenance system would need to retract or update inferences when objectStruct definitions change. In practice, strong schema changes might be infrequent, but the model is flexible enough to handle them at runtime. Documenting schema changes and possibly versioning objectStruct definitions can help maintain consistent reasoning, especially in long-running sessions.

**Type-Theoretic Interpretation:** In type theory terms, an **objectStruct** corresponds to a *type* (specifically, a record or product type) whose components are the fields defined by its fieldStructs. If objectStruct O has fields f1: T1, f2: T2, ..., fn: Tn (each Ti being the data type of field fi), we can view O as a tuple type or Cartesian product T1 × T2 × ... × Tn (with some fields possibly marked optional)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_type#:~:text=In%20many%20languages%2C%20product%20types,isomorphic%20to%20a%20product%20type)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_type#:~:text=In%20call,in%20the%20category%20of%20types). Each recordStruct of that type would then be an *instance* of this product type (i.e. a tuple of actual values). In many programming languages and logical systems, such a collection of labeled fields is exactly a **record type**[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_type#:~:text=In%20many%20languages%2C%20product%20types,isomorphic%20to%20a%20product%20type). This connection means one can apply standard type-theoretic reasoning: for instance, adding a new field f\_{n+1}: T\_{n+1} to objectStruct O conceptually changes the type to T1 × ... × Tn × T\_{n+1} – existing record instances of O would need to be interpreted as having an additional component (which could be considered a default or undefined value initially). Optional fields can be modeled as having a type T\_i ∪ {⊥} (i.e., a sum type of the real type and a special “no value” marker) to make every field total on each instance. Under the **Curry-Howard correspondence**, the conjunction of facts represented by all fields of an object is analogous to a logical AND of propositions[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_type#:~:text=algebraic%20data%20types%20with%20one,isomorphic%20to%20a%20product%20type). For example, saying a record has field1 \= value1 **and** field2 \= value2, etc., corresponds to asserting multiple atomic facts that all hold for that object (hence the whole record can be seen as a conjunction of attribute-value assertions). In category theory, we can think of an objectStruct as an object in a category (or a set in the category of Sets) and each fieldStruct as a morphism (function) projecting an instance to a value in the field’s domain. Specifically, if we denote by **Inst(O)** the set of all possible record instances of objectStruct O, then for each fieldStruct f: Ti (meaning f has data type Ti), there is a partial function f: Inst(O) → Ti. If f is total (required for all instances), this is a total function; if f is optional, it can be seen as a total function into Ti ∪ {⊥} or as a partially defined function. These functions (fields) collectively characterize the object type. In categorical terms, if we treat optionality properly, each objectStruct with *n* fields defines (or is isomorphic to) the product of its field types in an appropriate category (for partial functions one might use a category of sets with partial morphisms or treat absent values via a Maybe monad or similar construction).

**Generative and Evolutionary Considerations:** Because objectStructs are first-class data, an AI agent can use them to **generate code or interfaces** dynamically. For instance, given an objectStruct definition, an agent could programmatically generate a class or struct in a target programming language with corresponding fields, or generate a JSON schema or GraphQL type. The clarity of objectStruct’s definition (names and types of each field) directly feeds such code generation. The model supports *schema evolution*: adding a new fieldStruct to an objectStruct is akin to adding a new column to a class or table, but can be done on the fly. An agent reasoning about consistency will include checks like “if a new field is added to objectStruct O, ensure all existing records of O either get a default value or handle the lack of value appropriately (if the field is required, either prevent adding it retroactively or fill defaults; if optional, it’s fine to be missing on old records).” Tools could be built to automatically backfill or validate records when schema changes (this is outside the core model but a practical extension for maintaining truth: e.g., *if field added with a non-null constraint, then all current records must be assigned a value for it or marked as violating constraints until fixed*).

**Validation Rules (objectStruct):** To ensure an AI’s understanding, here are some key rules and checks involving objectStructs:

* *Type-Field Consistency:* **If** an objectStruct O is defined, **then** for every recordStruct r with Type(r)=O and every fieldStruct f owned by O, either r has at most one value for f or (if f is optional) possibly no value. Conversely, **if** r has a value for some fieldStruct f, **then** Owner(f) (the objectStruct that defines f) *must equal* Type(r)[\[1\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=)[\[2\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=Stores%20the%20possible%20attributes%20that,an%20entity%20can%20have). *(In other words, records cannot have values for fields that their type doesn’t define.)* Any violation (a rogue field in a record of a different type) indicates a data inconsistency.

* *Required Field Coverage:* **If** objectStruct O defines a fieldStruct f as required, **then for every** recordStruct r with Type(r)=O, **there exists** a value assignment for f in r (i.e. r contains field f with some value). If such an r lacks a value for f, the dataset is incomplete or violates the schema integrity. An agent should flag this as an error or an unknown that must be resolved (depending on whether we treat it as a violation or just missing info in an open-world sense).

* *Uniqueness (Type-wide):* **If** objectStruct O has a fieldStruct u marked as unique (serving as a key or unique property), **then** no two distinct recordStructs of type O may share the same value for u. Formally, for any two records r1, r2 of type O, if both have a value for field u, we must not have Val(r1, u) \= Val(r2, u) unless r1 \= r2. If a unique field is optional, records lacking a value for u pose no conflict (though if uniqueness is meant as a primary identifier, usually it’d be required as well). This invariant ensures identity or key integrity within the type.

* *Field Listing Completeness:* **If** an objectStruct O is known to the agent, the agent should be aware of all fieldStructs currently defined for O. In practice, the agent can maintain a list of fields per type. A *minimal falsification check* here is: *If the agent believes field f belongs to O, then querying the schema (objectStruct–fieldStruct mapping) should confirm f is listed under O.* If the agent finds a field value in a record of type O that is not in that list, it indicates the knowledge base is outdated (perhaps a new field was added that the agent didn’t register). The agent should then update its schema understanding by fetching the new objectStruct definition (or the fieldStruct list). This ensures the agent’s view of the intensional schema remains consistent with the actual state of the database.

By upholding these rules, the **objectStruct** layer provides a robust backbone for the schema, enabling dynamic yet consistent extension of the data model.

## **fieldStruct** (Field/Attribute Definition)

**Role & Definition:** A **fieldStruct** represents a *field definition* – essentially the metadata for a property/attribute of an objectStruct. In relational terms, it’s analogous to a column definition (but decoupled from a fixed table), and in object terms, it’s like a class data member or property descriptor. Each fieldStruct defines **what** kind of data can be associated with a particular aspect of an object, including its *name*, *data type*, *constraints*, and *ownership (which objectStruct it belongs to)*[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=,The%20value%20of%20the%20attribute). FieldStructs are intensional entities: they don’t hold actual data themselves, but rather define the slots where data will go in recordStructs. They allow the schema to be self-descriptive – for example, an AI agent can read a fieldStruct to know that “Persons have an Age field of type Integer, required, with allowed range 0-120”. In the Oblio model, fieldStructs make the system *metadata-driven*: the behavior of data (type checking, validation rules, etc.) is driven by these definitions rather than being hardcoded into application logic[\[6\]](https://dzone.com/articles/custom-attributes-in-relational-databases#:~:text=Concept)[\[13\]](https://dzone.com/articles/custom-attributes-in-relational-databases#:~:text=CREATE%20TABLE%20EntityAttrValue%20,id%29).

**Structure and Attributes:** Each fieldStruct contains a set of properties that describe a field:

* **Name:** A human-readable name or identifier for the field (unique within its owning objectStruct, as noted). This is how the field is referenced in queries or code (e.g., “Age”, “Title”, “Salary”). It’s essentially the label of the attribute.

* **Owner (Object Type):** A reference to the objectStruct that this fieldStruct is a part of. This links the field definition to its context. For instance, fieldStruct “Salary” might have Owner \= objectStruct “Job” if only Job entities have a Salary. In a physical schema, this could be an object\_type\_id foreign key stored in the FieldStruct metadata table. As discussed, this owner relationship is one-to-many: one objectStruct to many fieldStructs.

* **Data Type (Domain):** The datatype or domain of values that this field can take. This could be a primitive type (integer, float, text, boolean, date, etc.), or a reference type (pointing to another objectStruct’s records), or even a complex type (list, set, JSON, etc.), depending on the system’s capabilities. The data type might be stored as a code or reference (for primitive types) or possibly as a link to another objectStruct (if modeling a foreign key relationship). For example, fieldStruct “BirthDate” might have dataType \= “Date”, whereas fieldStruct “Employer” might have dataType \= “Reference\<Company\>” indicating it should hold an identifier for a Company record.

* **Cardinality / Multiplicity:** This indicates whether the field is single-valued or multi-valued for a given record. A single-valued field means each record can have at most one value for this attribute (the usual case, analogous to one column per row). A multi-valued field (if supported) would allow a record to have a set or list of values for that attribute (analogous to one-to-many relationship or an array of values). In a pure EAV implementation, multi-valued attributes are typically handled by multiple rows in the value table for the same entity and attribute. The fieldStruct could carry a flag like “allowMultiple \= true/false”. For example, a field “PhoneNumber” could be marked multi-valued if an individual can have multiple phone numbers. If multi-valued, each entry is still of the specified data type (e.g., each phone number is a string), and the agent must treat the set of values collectively as the attribute’s value.

* **Constraints & Validation Rules:** FieldStruct may include various constraints:

* **Required:** A boolean indicating if a value *must* be provided for this field for every record of the owning type (unless under open-world reasoning it’s temporarily unknown, but ultimately it should exist). Required \= true typically implies the field cannot be left null/blank (for each record, at least one (entity, field, value) triple must exist)[\[14\]](https://dzone.com/articles/custom-attributes-in-relational-databases#:~:text=,validation%20and%20evolution).

* **Unique:** Whether the field’s value must be unique across all records of the owning objectStruct (making it a candidate key or part of one). If Unique \= true, the database or agent must enforce that no two records share the same value for this field (unless the field is empty for one, and even then, usually at most one record can have a given value).

* **Default Value:** An optional default to use if a record is created without specifying this field. This could be a literal (e.g., default status \= “New”) or a formula. Defaults are useful for the agent to auto-populate missing values on new records or to treat unspecified fields as having some implicit value (though in an open-world logical sense, a default is more a convenience than a truth – it’s a way to fill the unknown with a presumably intended value).

* **Domain Constraints:** These include data type validations (like max length for strings[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=,The%20value%20of%20the%20attribute), regex patterns, min/max for numbers, allowed enum values, etc.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=the%20following%20columns%3A%20an%20attribute,The%20value%20of%20the%20attribute)) and possibly relational constraints (like if it’s a reference, maybe a cascade delete rule or required existence of target).

* **Semantic Constraints:** Possibly more complex rules, such as “if field X is set, field Y must be after date in X” or other cross-field rules. These are not inherent in fieldStruct alone but can be encoded as part of a schema logic that the agent knows.

All these properties together define the field’s *intension*. For instance, a fieldStruct might be represented as: *Field ID \= 42, Name \= “Age”, OwnerType \= PersonType, DataType \= Integer, Required \= false, Unique \= false, MinValue \= 0, MaxValue \= 150*. This tells the agent everything needed to validate and work with “Age” values for Person records.

**Relationship to Other Components:** By design:

* A **fieldStruct** is *owned by* exactly one **objectStruct** (its Owner). This one-to-many relationship (one object type has many fields) was described earlier. The fieldStruct effectively *inherits context* from its owner: e.g., “Age” means “Person.Age” if Person is the owner. There is no fieldStruct that exists outside an objectStruct; if a property is applicable to multiple types, typically it would be duplicated per type or modeled in a different way (like a shared parent type or a generic key-value mechanism). This ensures clarity in the schema: every field has a well-defined domain of applicability.

* A **fieldStruct** is *referenced by* potentially many **recordStruct** values. For each fieldStruct, there may be zero, one, or many actual (record, value) pairs stored for it – each record of the appropriate type can contribute at most one value (unless multi-valued) for that field. In the physical EAV table, attrId or equivalent would point to the fieldStruct (attribute metadata)[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=,The%20value%20of%20the%20attribute), and many rows may have the same attrId (meaning many records have values for that attribute)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=This%20data%20representation%20is%20analogous,to%20the%20few%20columns). From the perspective of a fieldStruct, one can imagine an inverted index: “FieldStruct F has values in records {r1, r2, ..., rk}.” This is the many-to-many linkage realized by the value table (Field \<-\> Record via Value). The agent can thus answer queries like “list all values of field F across all records” by scanning the relevant triples.

* FieldStruct to **Value Domain**: If the dataType of a field is a reference to another objectStruct (i.e., a foreign key relationship), then each value for this field should correspond to some recordStruct of the target type. The relationship here is that the fieldStruct *encodes* a relationship between objectStructs. For example, suppose fieldStruct “employer” belongs to objectStruct “Person” and has dataType \= Reference of objectStruct “Company”. Then whenever a Person record has an “employer” value, that value should be the unique ID of a Company record. The fieldStruct serves as the schema for a link from Person to Company. In terms of data integrity, a value for this field is valid only if it references an existing Company record (enforcing referential integrity). The agent should be aware of such reference types and perhaps treat them specially (like enabling join-like reasoning or graph traversal along these links).

* FieldStruct and **objectStruct hierarchy**: If objectStructs had inheritance, fieldStructs might be inherited too. Since we assume no direct inheritance in the base model, we won’t digress, but if, say, objectStruct B inherits A, then fieldStructs of A would implicitly apply to B. This could be modeled by duplicating fieldStructs for B or by logic that says “if not found in B, use A’s field by name” etc. For now, each fieldStruct is tied only to one objectStruct.

**Implicit Invariants and Normalization:** FieldStructs enable a high degree of normalization and consistency:

* **Attribute Metadata Integrity:** Every fieldStruct must have a valid Owner reference (cannot point to a non-existent objectStruct) and a valid data type definition. The agent should ensure no dangling references – e.g., if an objectStruct is removed, its fieldStructs should be removed or reassigned as well to maintain consistency. The design is such that *field metadata is separated from actual values*, which avoids repeating type or constraint info in each record. This is part of what makes EAV space-efficient for sparse data[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=)[\[19\]](https://www.dremio.com/wiki/entity-attribute-value-model/#:~:text=The%20EAV%20model%20is%20essentially,structured%20or%20sparse%20data): rather than having many null columns or repeated columns across tables, you have one centralized definition. It’s critical that an agent never conflates the field definition with field instance values; changes to a fieldStruct (like correcting a dataType or adding a constraint) affect interpretation of all associated values.

* **Name Uniqueness & Stability:** As mentioned, field names are unique per object type. Also, ideally once a fieldStruct is created, its identity (ID) remains stable even if the name is changed (if the system allows renaming) – because the ID may be used in stored data. If a name changes, all references (including agent’s internal knowledge) should update the label, but the underlying ID or key continues to match existing record entries. The agent should handle the possibility of such schema evolution (e.g., field “Address” is renamed to “MailingAddress”; the agent should not treat them as two separate fields but the same one with a new label).

* **No Duplicate Field Definitions:** There should not be two fieldStructs under the same objectStruct with the same name or serving the exact same purpose. This prevents redundancy and confusion. If accidentally two were made, one should be retired. The agent could detect if two fields of one type have the same meaning and raise a normalization concern. This is more of a design guideline – the system should enforce name uniqueness anyway.

* **One Field, One Purpose:** Each fieldStruct ideally represents one atomic property (following normalization principles). If a field needs to store multiple pieces of data, it should likely be split into multiple fields. For example, instead of a single “Address” field containing city, state, zip in one string, one might have separate fields. This atomicity makes querying and reasoning easier (the agent can reason about each piece separately). The intensional design encourages thinking in terms of fine-grained attributes.

**Operational Semantics (How fieldStructs affect data):**

When data is added or updated, the fieldStruct governs how it’s processed: \- **Inserting a Value:** When an application or agent inserts a value for a field (say setting *Person.Age \= 30* on a record), the system uses the fieldStruct to validate the operation. It checks: does fieldStruct “Age” exist for objectStruct “Person”? Yes – proceed. Is 30 of type Integer? Yes (given Age’s dataType). Is Age required (if inserting a new record)? If so, ensure it’s provided (we are providing it). Is it within allowed range? Yes, 30 is between 0 and 150\. Any triggers or default interplay? (Not in this simple set operation.) Then it writes an EAV triple: (recordID, fieldID-for-Age, value=30) to the storage. The fieldStruct’s ID is what gets stored in the attrId column[\[13\]](https://dzone.com/articles/custom-attributes-in-relational-databases#:~:text=CREATE%20TABLE%20EntityAttrValue%20,id%29), tying that value to the schema. If any validation fails (say we tried to set Age \= “thirty” which is not an integer), the operation is rejected. Thus, fieldStruct acts as a contract and gatekeeper for data integrity.

* **Updating Schema (fieldStruct changes):** If a fieldStruct’s definition changes (e.g., dataType changed from Integer to String, or it’s now marked required), the effect on existing data can be significant. An agent should deduce certain consequences: if dataType changes, all existing values must be convertible to the new type, or else those values become invalid/inconsistent. If a field is now required, any existing record missing it breaks the rule (unless one decides the rule only applies henceforth). In a rigorous system, schema changes might trigger migration or validation passes. For instance, if we mark “Email” as required for Person, the agent might need to check all Person records and possibly fill a default or report which ones violate the new constraint. This dynamic nature means an AI agent responsible for data quality must constantly enforce the fieldStruct constraints on the record data whenever either side changes.

* **Querying by Field:** FieldStructs allow queries like “find all records where Field X has value Y”. The agent or database can use the field’s ID or name to filter the EAV table. For example, to find all persons aged 30, one looks up fieldStruct ID for “Age” under Person type, then finds all triples where attrId \= Age’s ID and value \= 30, then retrieves the corresponding records[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=This%20data%20representation%20is%20analogous,to%20the%20few%20columns). Because values are stored in a generic table, such queries can be less straightforward (in SQL, this is a self-join or pivot scenario). However, the presence of field metadata means we can prepare optimized queries or even generate ORM-like property access. An AI could generate a SQL join dynamically using the field definitions it knows. Under partial knowledge conditions, if some records lack that field, they simply won’t appear in the EAV table, meaning the query naturally ignores them (again, absence means “no assertion” \= unknown or irrelevant, as opposed to false).

* **Continuous Truth and Partial Knowledge for Fields:** If an agent is reasoning about incomplete data, fieldStructs define the *potential* truth that could be asserted. For example, consider a rule: “If a Person has a DateOfDeath field filled, then that implies the Person is not alive.” If for a given Person record the DateOfDeath is unknown (no value present), the agent cannot conclude anything about that person’s status – the truth of “has DateOfDeath” is unknown (open-world perspective). Only when a value is provided (the fact exists) does the agent derive the implication. FieldStructs help here by providing the vocabulary of possible facts. The agent can frame logical predicates like HasValue(record, Field) or actual Value(record, Field) \= X. Under continuous knowledge updates, new field values might appear (someone enters a DateOfDeath for a person), turning a previously unknown fact into a known fact, which triggers new inferences. The model supports this gracefully: adding a new (record, field, value) triple is simply populating an existing slot defined by the fieldStruct. The truth maintenance system should handle that the property “HasValue(person123, DateOfDeath)” went from false (or unknown) to true, and any dependent rules fire. If a field value is retracted (deleted), the agent should then consider that fact as no longer true – unless perhaps a default is considered (but typically, deletion means unknown again or no such fact). The presence of fieldStruct means even if a value is missing, the agent *knows that such a property exists in the schema*, so it may anticipate that a value could later appear. This is akin to reasoning with predicates that might later be asserted.

* **Logical Interpretation:** We can treat each fieldStruct as a logical predicate or function symbol. For instance, a fieldStruct “Age” of Person can be seen as a function Age(person) \= value or a set of facts Age(PersonID, Value). In a logic database, one might have a predicate Age(PersonID, Value) for each person who has an age recorded. If person 7’s age is 30, we have the fact Age(7, 30\). If person 8 has no age on record, the predicate Age(8, X) has no grounding – which under open-world means we just don’t know it. Under closed-world, one might say Age(8, X) is false for all X (meaning “no age”), which obviously is not semantically right – hence open-world fits better for missing attributes. An AI reasoner can also use the field’s domain to constrain reasoning: if it’s known Age is an integer field, it will not consider non-integer possibilities for that predicate. If Employer is a reference to Company, the reasoner will only consider values that are valid Company IDs for that predicate, and perhaps even use knowledge about companies when reasoning on people (like join operations or graph traversals).

**Type-Theoretic & Category-Theoretic View:** Each **fieldStruct** can be viewed as a *typed slot* or a *partial function* associated with an object type. In a simply-typed lambda calculus sense, if we have a type Person (from objectStruct) and a field Age: Person \-\> Integer, then Age is akin to a function symbol of type Person → Integer? (the question mark indicates it might be undefined for some individuals if optional). This is exactly how record types are modeled: a record type is a labeled product of field types, and each field label is a projection function. Category-theoretically, if we consider a category **C** where objects are *entity instances* and morphisms represent *attribute values*, it’s more natural to think in Set theory: The set of all Person instances might be denoted as Inst(Person). A field f: T (with T a set of possible values) can be considered a morphism (actually a set-theoretic function) f: Inst(Person) → T if total. If not all persons have a value, one formalization is a partial function, or we embed it into a total function f: Inst(Person) → T ∪ {⊥} by adding a special “undefined” symbol. Another approach is to say each field induces a relation: a subset of Inst(Person) × T such that (person, value) ∈ relation if that person has that value for the field. This relational view aligns with the EAV storage: the triples table essentially stores these relations for each field. Each fieldStruct corresponds to one relation (one could imagine splitting the big EAV table by attribute, yielding many small tables, each containing pairs of (entity, value) for that attribute). But the unified design uses one table with a field identifier column to indicate which relation a row belongs to[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=This%20data%20representation%20is%20analogous,to%20the%20few%20columns).

From a **logical standpoint**, a fieldStruct is like a predicate symbol (unary or binary depending how you see it: unary if we think of it as a function from entity to value, binary if we represent the relationship between an entity and a value explicitly). Each record’s field value yields an atomic formula like FieldName(Entity, Value). If we treat field names as binary predicates, then the collection of all such facts for a given field is the extension of that predicate. Under intensional/extensional database terminology, the set of all fieldStructs and objectStructs define the intensional database (like predicates), and the recordStruct values populate the extensional database (the facts)[\[20\]](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022000014000129#:~:text=ScienceDirect%20www,sugar%20in%20the%20previous)[\[21\]](https://documentserver.uhasselt.be/bitstream/1942/20759/1/4054%20D-2013-2451-15%20Tom%20ameloot.pdf#:~:text=2The%20abbreviation%20%E2%80%9Cidb%E2%80%9D%20stands%20for,relation%20names). The agent can use this analogy to apply techniques from knowledge representation: e.g., consistency checking akin to schema constraints, or query answering akin to relational division (finding records that have a certain combination of fields matching criteria)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=).

**Examples to Clarify:** Suppose we have objectStruct **Car** with fieldStructs: “Make” (type Text, required), “Model” (Text, required), “Year” (Integer, required, range 1886-2025), “PreviousOwners” (Integer, optional, default 0), “Features” (Text, multi-valued, optional). \- The fieldStruct “Year” might have: Name \= Year, Type \= Integer, Constraint: min=1886 (first car invention year), max=2025, Required \= true. \- “PreviousOwners”: Name \= PreviousOwners, Type \= Integer, default \= 0, not required (so if not provided, default 0 implies first owner). \- “Features”: Name \= Features, Type \= Text, multi-valued \= true, meaning a Car record can have multiple Feature values (like “Sunroof”, “GPS”, etc.).

For any given Car record, the agent expects it to have exactly one Make, one Model, one Year (due to required), optionally a PreviousOwners (if not given, treat as 0 by default), and zero or many Feature entries. The fieldStruct definitions allow the agent to enforce that Year is a four-digit number in range, and that Features are just free text tags. If a Car record came in with two Year values, that violates cardinality (since Year is not multi-valued, at most one per car). The agent would flag that as an inconsistency. If a Car record has no Year, that’s violating a required field – the agent might treat that as incomplete data that must be resolved (maybe the record shouldn’t exist or needs updating). If a Car has a PreviousOwners value of “John” (a string), that violates type (expects Integer), so either the data entry is wrong or the field type is wrong. This is how fieldStruct guides validation.

**Validation Rules (fieldStruct):** The following checks help ensure an agent’s understanding and usage of fieldStructs is correct:

* *Ownership and Typing:* **If** a value triple (record R, field F, value V) exists, **then** it must satisfy: (1) Owner(F) \= Type(R) (the field’s owner type matches the record’s type), and (2) V ∈ Dom(F) (the value belongs to the field’s declared data type domain). For instance, if F expects a Date, V must be a valid date value (or a representation convertible to Date)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=,The%20value%20of%20the%20attribute). If either condition is false, the triple is invalid. An agent should never knowingly assert or accept a fact that breaks these conditions. This rule ties together objectStruct, fieldStruct, and recordStruct in one of the most fundamental invariants of the model[\[1\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=)[\[2\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=Stores%20the%20possible%20attributes%20that,an%20entity%20can%20have).

* *Uniqueness and Keys:* **If** a fieldStruct F is marked Unique, **then** for any two triples (r1, F, v) and (r2, F, v) with the same value v, it must be that r1 and r2 refer to the *same* record (i.e., r1 \= r2). The agent can enforce this by checking new inserts against existing values index. If F is also Required and Unique, it essentially can serve as a primary key for the objectStruct (each record has exactly one F and all are distinct). If F is Unique but optional, then at most one record can omit it (if we treat null vs null, usually uniqueness rules treat null as “not equal to anything”, so many can omit; the agent should clarify how to handle missing in uniqueness – often missing values are exempt from uniqueness constraints). For safety, the agent can assume that uniqueness is only checked for actual provided values.

* *Required Values:* **If** a fieldStruct F is Required for owner type O, **then** for every record r of type O, a triple (r, F, v) must exist (some value must be present). Absence of such a triple means r is in violation. In logical terms, ∀r: Type(r)=O ⇒ ∃v: Value(r,F)=v. This is a constraint the agent must strive to maintain or at least report as an inconsistency until resolved. The agent might proactively fill defaults if available rather than leaving it blank.

* *Multiplicity:* **If** a fieldStruct F is single-valued (not multi), **then** there should not exist two distinct triples (r, F, v1) and (r, F, v2) for the same record r (with v1 ≠ v2). In other words, a record cannot have two different values for the same field. If F is multi-valued, multiple triples per record are allowed, but possibly with additional constraints (e.g., if the field is multi but the values must all be distinct, the agent should ensure no duplicate value entries for the same record and field).

* *Referential Integrity:* **If** a fieldStruct F has dataType \= Reference to objectStruct O2, **then** for any triple (r1, F, v) where r1 is of type Owner(F) (say O1), the value v should correspond to a valid record ID of type O2. Formally, ∃ a recordStruct r2 such that ID(r2) \= v and Type(r2) \= O2. If no such r2 exists, the value is a dangling reference – invalid in a consistent state. The agent must either prevent insertion of such a value or at least mark it as an error to be cleaned up. This rule effectively enforces that foreign keys point to existing records, akin to a SQL foreign key constraint. An AI reasoner should thus treat Value(r1, F, r2\_id) as implying the existence of record r2. In a knowledge graph analogy, this says if there’s an edge labeled F from node r1 to node v, v must exist as a node of type O2 (unless using open-world where maybe v could be an as-yet-unknown entity, but typically in a database, we don’t allow references to non-existent IDs).

* *Domain Constraints Checking:* For each fieldStruct, all associated values should satisfy its specific validation rules. For example, if F has a regex pattern constraint, **then** ∀ triples (r, F, v), the string v should match the regex. If F has a numerical range, each numeric value should lie in that range. The agent should apply these checks on data entry and possibly during data audits. If the system stores these constraints formally (which it should, as part of fieldStruct metadata[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=,The%20value%20of%20the%20attribute)), an AI can reason about them (e.g., it might deduce that if Age’s max is 150, and a rule says “if Age \> 18 then isAdult \= true”, it knows Age is always ≤150 so that’s a safe bound).

* *No Orphan FieldStruct:* A fieldStruct without an owning objectStruct or with zero usage might be suspect. Although it’s possible to define a field and not yet have any record with that field (especially if optional and no one has filled it out, or no records of that type exist yet), a fieldStruct should not exist if its objectStruct has been deleted. The agent should consider it an invariant that if an objectStruct is removed, all its fieldStructs should be removed too (to avoid orphan metadata that doesn’t apply to any type). Similarly, if a fieldStruct is removed (schema evolution), ideally all triples referencing it in records should be cleaned up or marked obsolete – otherwise, those become orphan data (facts about a field that the schema no longer recognizes). This hints at the need for **schema-versioned truth** management: the truth of a fact Value(r, F, v) can itself become invalid if F ceases to exist in schema (the agent might then interpret that as an unknown predicate or disregard it in queries).

To summarize, **fieldStructs** serve as the controlled vocabulary and rulebook for all attributes in the system. They ensure that every piece of data in **recordStructs** is interpretable and validated, and they enable the flexibility to add new properties as needed at runtime[\[23\]](https://dzone.com/articles/custom-attributes-in-relational-databases#:~:text=Concept). By following the above constraints, an AI agent can maintain consistency between the intensional schema level and the extensional data level, and leverage fieldStruct metadata for intelligent behaviors (like automated UI generation, consistent data validation, or inferencing new facts from known attribute values).

## **recordStruct** (Record / Entity Instance Representation)

**Role & Definition:** A **recordStruct** represents an *individual entity instance* – a single “record” or object – within the Oblio data model. It is the extensional counterpart to an objectStruct: whereas objectStruct defines a type (schema), a recordStruct is a concrete occurrence of that type with actual data (values for some or all of the defined fields). In a traditional database, this would correspond to a row in a table; in an ORM, it’s an instantiated object (often called an entity or model instance). However, since the schema here is dynamic, a recordStruct doesn’t have a fixed set of columns in a fixed table. Instead, each recordStruct can be thought of as an *aggregated collection of attribute-value pairs* (each pair linking to a fieldStruct) plus an identity and type label. In practice, a recordStruct is often identified by a unique **Record ID** and a **Type reference** (link to an objectStruct), and its data is stored as a set of entries in the EAV value table associating that record ID with field IDs and values[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=Data%20is%20recorded%20as%20three,columns). The recordStruct itself may be an abstract notion or an in-memory object that lazily pulls in those field values. For conceptual clarity, we treat recordStruct as having *slots* for each field defined by its objectStruct – those slots may be filled or not, and the filled ones correspond to actual stored facts.

**Composition and Content:** A recordStruct instance r of type O can be viewed as a tuple of values (v1, v2, ..., vn) for the fields \[f1, f2, ..., fn\] defined in O – but with the allowance that some vi may be “not provided” (if the field is optional and not set for this record). In other words, each recordStruct has: \- A **Record ID** (likely a numeric or GUID primary key that uniquely distinguishes it among all records, or at least unique within its type). \- A **Type tag** (the objectStruct it instantiates, e.g., PersonType ID 5). \- A set of **Field Values**: zero or more triples of the form (Field \= Value) for fields defined in its type. Each such triple corresponds to a fieldStruct of that type and a value assigned. If a field is optional and not set, it simply doesn’t appear in this set (its slot is conceptually empty or null). If a field is multi-valued, it can appear multiple times with different values. \- Optionally, possibly some **system fields** like creation timestamp, last update timestamp, etc., that every record might have regardless of type (these would be analogous to universal fields applicable to all objectStructs, possibly handled separately).

The recordStruct can thus be seen as containing references to fieldStruct definitions and actual data for each. For example, a recordStruct for objectStruct “Person” might internally look like: {Type=Person, ID=123, Fields \= \[(Name \= "Alice"), (Age \= 30), (Employer \= Company\#77)\]} indicating it’s a Person record with Name and Age provided and Employer referencing Company record \#77, and perhaps it doesn’t have, say, the optional MiddleName field.

**Relation to objectStruct and fieldStruct:**

* **Instance-of Relationship:** Every recordStruct r has an associated objectStruct O \= Type(r). This is often implemented as a foreign key in the record table pointing to the objectStruct metadata table. The *instance-of* relation is fundamental: it means r should obey all schema rules of O. The record knows what type it is, so the agent can infer which fieldStructs are permissible. The *set of field slots* for r is defined exactly by the fieldStructs of O. If O has n fields in its schema, then conceptually r has n potential slots (some filled, some empty). This is akin to an object-oriented instance containing members defined by its class.

* **Field values association:** A recordStruct is associated with fieldStructs through the values it carries. We can say a recordStruct *contains* a fieldStruct F if it has a value for F (i.e., there exists a triple linking the record and F). More precisely, one might say *recordStruct R realizes fieldStruct F with value V* if (R, F, V) is present in the data store. If a field is not present, one could say the record has no value for that field (which is not the same as a null value unless a null is explicitly stored; typically in EAV, absence \= null implicitly). Thus, the many-to-many relationship between records and fields (via values) can be seen from the record’s side: each recordStruct may be linked to many fieldStructs (up to the number defined in its type) by having values, and each fieldStruct can link to many records via values. The combination of record ID and field ID uniquely identifies a fact (assuming at most one value per record-field, or an ordering if multiple).

* **Identification and References:** RecordStructs can reference each other if fields are of reference types. For example, if Person record 123 has Employer field \= Company record 77, then record 123 *references* record 77 through that field. In a graph interpretation, recordStructs are nodes and fieldStruct references are labeled edges. The agent can traverse these references to answer questions like “who is Alice’s employer?” or “list employees of Company 77” (the latter would require scanning all Person records for those whose Employer field \= 77). These references do not change the basic containment though: Person\#123 contains fieldStruct “Employer” as part of its data, with value pointing to Company\#77. It’s one record containing a reference to another record, as governed by the field’s definition.

**Invariants and Data Integrity Constraints:** RecordStructs are where all schema rules meet reality. Key invariants include:

* **Type Matching:** *If a recordStruct r has any field value for fieldStruct f, then it must be true that Type(r) \= Owner(f).* This reiterates a rule from earlier, from the record’s viewpoint: a record cannot have values for fields that are not defined by its objectStruct[\[1\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=)[\[2\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=Stores%20the%20possible%20attributes%20that,an%20entity%20can%20have). This is the most fundamental integrity rule linking intensional and extensional levels. An agent should never assign or allow a value for (record, field) if the field’s owner type doesn’t match the record’s type. In practice, the system enforces this by only considering fieldStructs from the appropriate type when editing or creating record data.

* **No Missing Required Fields (Consistency):** *If Type(r) \= O and objectStruct O has a required fieldStruct f, then record r must contain a value for f.* This is the counterpart of the fieldStruct’s required rule, now at instance level. For each record, check all required fields of its type – each should have an entry. If any is missing, the record is incomplete or invalid. In a strictly enforced system, such a record would not be allowed to persist (the transaction to insert it would be rejected). In a more permissive system (or during schema evolution), a temporarily missing required field might be flagged for later fulfillment. From an AI perspective, if a required field is missing, the agent should treat it as an inconsistency or an unknown that *must* eventually be known for the record to be considered complete. Perhaps it would prompt for that information or infer a placeholder.

* **Single-valued Field Uniqueness:** *For each record r and each single-valued field f of Type(r), there exists at most one value entry (r,f,v).* This simply means a record can’t have two different values for the same single-valued field (no duplicate attribute entries). In the data model, this is naturally enforced if the primary key of the EAV table is (recordID, fieldID)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=This%20data%20representation%20is%20analogous,to%20the%20few%20columns) – which ensures only one row per combination. If the system doesn’t enforce it at storage, the agent must logically assume it (and if evidence of a duplicate arises, that signals a violation). If a field is multi-valued, the key might include a value ID, but for single-valued, (record, field) should be unique. So a minimal check: ensure no record has two triples with the same fieldStruct.

* **Value Type Correctness:** *If a record r contains (r, f, v), then v must be of the correct data type for field f.* This was already covered under fieldStruct invariants, but it’s worth restating: record data must adhere to the types. The agent should consider a record invalid if any of its values is of wrong type (e.g., a text in an integer field). Ideally, such a situation is prevented at entry, but if the agent is doing auditing or integration, it might encounter it and then either convert or flag it.

* **Identity and Key Constraints:** If the objectStruct has a unique field or set of fields as a key, the record’s combination of those should be unique across all records of that type. For instance, if (FirstName, LastName, BirthDate) is a key for Person, then no two Person records should share all three values. For an agent, checking this might involve ensuring a new record doesn’t duplicate an existing record’s key fields (to avoid “duplicate entity” entries). If a duplicate is found, it could indicate either a violation or that those two records actually represent the same real-world entity (which might be a data quality issue or a merge candidate rather than strictly schema violation if the system doesn’t enforce it).

* **Record ID Uniqueness:** Each recordStruct has a unique ID. No two recordStructs (even of different types) share the same primary identifier (assuming a global identity space; if identities are only unique per type, then uniqueness must hold within type and a composite (type, id) is unique globally). This is a low-level constraint ensuring records are distinguishable. It also implies that given a (type, id) pair, the agent can locate at most one record.

* **Referential Integrity (Instance level):** If record r1 has a field value referencing record r2 (via a fieldStruct of reference type), then r2 should exist (and typically, remain in existence as long as r1’s reference exists). If r2 is deleted, ideally the reference in r1 should be cleared or r1 deleted too, to avoid dangling references. The agent should be mindful of cascading effects: e.g., if Company\#77 is deleted, any Person with Employer=77 now violates referential integrity. The agent might then consider those Person records as having an unknown or invalid Employer – which is a consistency problem to resolve (either remove that field value or assign a new valid reference). This invariant again aligns with maintaining truth: one should not have facts that point to non-things.

* **Optional Field Semantics:** If a field is optional and a record doesn’t have it, that’s acceptable (not a violation) as long as the field isn’t required. However, the agent might have rules about interpreting absence. In a closed-world setting, absence could be treated as a *negative fact* (e.g., “if there’s no value for Allergy for this patient, assume none” – dangerous unless explicitly the design). In an open-world or partial knowledge setting, absence means *no information*. The agent should maintain the distinction. An invariant might be: *The absence of a (record, field) in the data does not entail any explicit logical assertion, except that if the field had a default, one might implicitly use that.* Some systems actually materialize default values as real entries at record creation to avoid ambiguity. If Oblio does not, the agent itself might need to impute default on the fly.

* **Completeness vs Soundness:** In a scenario of continuous knowledge, we might define a concept of *complete record*. A recordStruct could be labeled *complete* if it has values for all required fields (and maybe some optional ones filled in if known). If not complete, the agent knows more data could come. For certain reasoning tasks, the agent may assume completeness for certain records (closed-world on that record) when appropriate. Managing this assumption is crucial: e.g., in a truth maintenance scenario, if a record becomes complete (all required fields filled), one might mark it as such. If later a new required field is added to the type, all records become incomplete again until they get that field’s value. The agent must then adjust any inferences that assumed completeness.

**Query and Behavior Semantics:**

* **Retrieving a Record:** To get the full information of a recordStruct, one typically queries all (recordID \= R) entries from the EAV table and joins with fieldStruct metadata to interpret each. For an AI agent, this means assembling a set of (field name, value) pairs from the raw triples. The agent might maintain an internal object or dictionary for r, mapping field names to values or sets of values. In an ORM-like usage, one might have a Record object with properties for each field. Since fields are dynamic, such an object might be a generic map or an object with dynamic attributes. The agent can generate such an object on the fly using the objectStruct schema.

* **Answering Queries about Data:** Because data is not stored in fixed columns, queries that combine multiple fields need careful formulation (often joining the EAV table to itself for each field). For example, “find all Person records where FirstName \= 'John' AND City \= 'London'” involves finding record IDs that have a field FirstName \= John and also have field City \= London. In relational algebra this is a *relational division* or intersection of sets of record IDs[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entity%E2%80%93attribute%E2%80%93value_model#:~:text=). An AI reasoning engine can do this by intersection of fact sets: it gets the set of records for FirstName John (all triples with FirstName and "John"), and the set for City London, and takes the intersection of record IDs. Because of the vertical structure, such multi-attribute queries are more expensive than in a single-table model, but the agent’s logic should accommodate it. The agent might even do query optimization: for instance, if one set is much smaller, iterate that and check the other condition via an index lookup.

* **Continuous Updates:** A recordStruct’s information can evolve: fields can be added (by assigning a new value for a previously empty field slot), updated (existing (r,f,v\_old) replaced with (r,f,v\_new)), or removed (delete (r,f,v)). Each such change is effectively an atomic fact change. The agent’s world model should update correspondingly. For example, if a Person’s Address field value is changed, the agent should reflect that the old Address fact is no longer true, and a new fact is true. Any rules depending on address (say a rule “if city is X then do Y”) need re-evaluation. If a field is removed (like clearing an optional field’s value), then a fact becomes unknown again for that record. Under open-world reasoning, it would then no longer trigger rules that require that fact. Under closed-world assumption in a particular context, one might treat removal as asserting a negative (e.g., person has no address now, if such an interpretation makes sense). The difference is subtle and context-dependent.

* **Partial Knowledge Representation:** If an AI agent has incomplete information for a record, it might explicitly mark some fields as unknown or pending. For example, the agent could internally represent record 123 as {Name="Alice", Age=30, Employer=Unknown} if Employer is a field but not yet known for that record. This is effectively a *closed-world placeholder* to indicate “we know this field exists but we don’t have a value”. Another approach is just not include any value for Employer and treat that logically as unknown. The agent must be consistent in how it uses such placeholders. If it expects to later fill them, it should treat them as neither true nor false in reasoning. For instance, if a rule is “Employer exists implies Person is employed”, and the Employer field is unknown, we cannot conclude Person is or isn’t employed. If the field was optional and might never be set, perhaps that rule doesn’t apply unless filled.

* **Aggregating and Deriving Knowledge:** The dynamic schema allows new fields to be added to records later. Suppose we add a new fieldStruct “Nickname” to objectStruct Person. Immediately, all existing Person recordStructs conceptually gain a new (empty) slot for Nickname. The agent should then consider that any Person record could now have a Nickname fact. If a query or rule involves Nickname, previously it might have been an invalid query (unknown field), now it’s valid but for most records currently false (unknown). So, in effect, adding a field is like adding a new predicate to the logic system, for which no records have facts yet (unless defaults are auto-filled). The agent’s knowledge base needs to incorporate this new predicate with an empty extension initially. It might also generate tasks like “maybe prompt users to fill nicknames” or just be aware that it’s largely empty. Conversely, dropping a field is like removing a predicate: all facts of that predicate become irrelevant or need reclassification. The agent should then remove or ignore all triples for that field from its knowledge base and alter any rules or queries that referred to it (or mark them invalid). This is a non-trivial operation in a live reasoning system.

**Formal Perspective:**

We can formalize a recordStruct’s data as a partial function: let Fields(O) be the set of fieldStructs for objectStruct O. For a record r of type O, we define a function Val\_r: Fields(O) \-\> ∪\_{f∈Fields(O)} Dom(f) (the union of all field domains, though each field maps to only its own domain actually). Val\_r(f) is defined if and only if record r has a value for field f; if defined, Val\_r(f) ∈ Dom(f). If f is not set for r, then Val\_r(f) is undefined (or we say Val\_r(f) \= ⊥). We also have a predicate HasValue(r,f) that is true iff Val\_r(f) is defined. Then: \- Required means: ∀r, for all required f ∈ Fields(Type(r)), HasValue(r,f) is true. \- Single-valued means: the function yields at most one value (by definition of function). \- Multi-valued fields can be seen by allowing Val\_r(f) to return a set of values (subset of Dom(f)) instead of a single value (or treat each distinct (r,f,v) as separate but then the function model doesn’t hold directly; better to model multi-valued as Val\_r(f) ⊆ Dom(f)). \- The entire database extension can be seen as a set of triples E \= { (r, f, v) | Val\_r(f) \= v is defined }. This E is basically the EAV table content.

Now, **continuous truth** could refer to the idea that E and even Fields(O) can change over time (with time as a continuous or discrete progression). If we imagine a sequence of states, each state has a set of objectStructs, fieldStructs, and records with values. As time goes on, this knowledge grows or changes. The *truth* of a statement like ∃v: Val\_r(f)=v (i.e. "field f has some value for record r") can change from false to true when a value is added, or true to false if a value is removed (assuming removal either means no current value – making it false/unknown). The agent might treat time/event as an input stream modifying the extensional dataset.

**Generative Code and Reasoning Utility:** For an AI agent, recordStructs are the concrete targets for action – creating a new entity, updating one, or reasoning about one. The agent could generate code structures (classes, structs) to represent a record of a particular objectStruct. For example, reading the schema of Person, it could create a Python class Person with attributes corresponding to each field (perhaps using \_\_getattr\_\_ magic for undefined at compile time attributes). Alternatively, the agent might forego static generation and use a generic record holder that references schema metadata for flexibility.

During **schema evolution**, if an agent generates code from schema, adding a new field would entail updating that code. If the agent itself is the one to evolve the schema (e.g., adding a field to satisfy some new data requirement it deduced), it should also consider updating any dependent code or rules that operate on records of that type. For instance, if it generates a form for data entry for type O, and now a new field is added, the form should be updated to include an input for that field.

**Validation Rules (recordStruct):** Summarizing key checks:

* *Type-Field Validity:* **If** (r, f, v) is present, **then** Type(r) \= Owner(f) (restating for emphasis, as this rule touches all three components and is critical[\[1\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=)). An agent can test a record’s data by iterating its fields and confirming each field’s owner matches the record’s type.

* *Completeness of Required Fields:* **For each** recordStruct r, let O \= Type(r). For every fieldStruct f of O with Required=true, check that ∃ some value such that (r,f,v) ∈ E. Flag if missing. E.g., “If recordStruct X contains fieldStruct Y, then Y must be defined in X’s objectStruct” is one check (which we covered), and conversely, “If fieldStruct Y is defined as required in X’s objectStruct, then X must contain Y” is the complementary rule.

* *At-most-one value per (r,f) for single fields:* **If** there exist two triples (r,f,v1) and (r,f,v2) with v1 ≠ v2, and fieldStruct f is not multi-valued, **then** there is a violation. The agent’s understanding should be that cannot happen if the system is consistent. If multi-valued, that scenario is allowed by design, though the agent might then consider if order matters or not (usually not, treat as set).

* *Referential integrity on instance:* **If** (r, f, v) and f is a reference to type O2, **then** there should exist some record r2 with ID(r2)=v and Type(r2)=O2. If at some point r2 is deleted, the agent must either remove (r,f,v) or mark it invalid. Ideally define that such a triple should not exist in the current state if r2 doesn’t. That is both a constraint and a reactive rule: deletion of r2 implies deletion or nullification of references to it.

* *Record existence vs field existence:* It's implied but worth noting: **If** a recordStruct r is deleted, **then** all triples (r, f, v) should also be removed (cascading delete on attribute values). There should be no stray facts about a non-existent record. For an agent, if it encounters a value referencing a recordID that no longer appears in the record list, that indicates a data integrity problem in deletion handling.

* *Non-duplication of records based on key fields:* Optionally, the agent can enforce that no two distinct records of the same type have identical values for the designated key field(s). This is not easily enforced in the EAV model without custom logic or indexes on combinations of field values, but an agent can check when adding or use a constraint solver. This ensures the uniqueness invariants from fieldStruct are realized at record level.

* *Type Consistency Over Time:* If records can change type (usually they do not; type is like class – rarely changed, perhaps only via a transform or error correction), then one must ensure that when a record’s type is changed, its field values are purged or transformed to match the new type. Typically, one doesn’t simply reassign type because the set of valid fields changes drastically. If it did, the safe operation is: remove all field values that are not in the new type’s schema (or store them elsewhere) and then maybe try to map overlapping fields. Since this is edge-case, we assume record’s type is fixed upon creation.

By adhering to these, recordStructs become reliable carriers of truth as dictated by the schema. They embody the *instances* that an AI will reason about, and so ensuring their integrity ensures the AI’s inferences are sound.

---

**Concluding Synthesis:** The interplay of **objectStruct**, **fieldStruct**, and **recordStruct** in Oblio’s design yields a powerful, flexible system:

* An **objectStruct** is like a *class or category*, defining *what attributes exist* for entities of that type (intensional schema element)[\[24\]](https://dev.to/dedawit/entity-attribute-value-eav-model-2ghg#:~:text=Represents%20the%20main%20object%20whose,attributes%20can%20vary%20over%20time). It’s the anchor for integrity rules and a handle for grouping records.
